questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Images of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of the Matrix Under Its Action
questions.problem: Let $A$ be a $m\times n$ matrix. What is the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of ${A}^{T}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First,  notice that ${A}^{T}$ is a $n\times m$ matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{m}$ by ${A}^{T}$ gives a linear combination of the columns of ${A}^{T}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ {a}_{1}^{T} & {a}_{2}^{T} & ⋯ & {a}_{m}^{T} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{T}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{m}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{1}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{2}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{m}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{m}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}),$ the column space of ${A}^{T},$ or equivalently, the row space of $A.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ is mapped to the zero vector $0$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}(({A}^{T})^{T})=\text{Col}(A)$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}).$

This can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14100016/assets/8ca8508d05e28e4c91b5a7f3c65826ce68b5dacd382bfb1a76f09c09d1d004bf.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Orthogonal Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix
questions.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Null}({B}^{T})$ for every matrix $B?$

- $\text{Null}(B)$
- $\text{Col}(B)$
- $\text{Col}({B}^{T})$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Null}({B}^{T})$ is the left null space of $B.$ This consists of vectors that, when pre-multiplied by ${B}^{T},$ result in the zero-vector $0.$

When pre-multiplying a vector by ${B}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${B}^{T}$, that is, each column of $B$, by that vector. So, $\text{Null}({B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the column space of $B,$ which is $\text{Col}(B).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $B$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14100016/assets/18713ed3d103ca0a02d74cede1e6448012e0aa28a2df804d41cfb277589a0158.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Images of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of the Matrix Under Its Action
questions.problem: Let $A$ be a $7\times 5$ matrix. What is the image of ${R}^{5}$ under the action of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{5}$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} & {a}_{4} & {a}_{5} \\ | & | & | & | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4} \\ {x}_{5}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{3} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{4} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{5}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{5} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{5}$ under the action of $A$ must be $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14100016/assets/889b83fadd26b377c4dd34143c9b16541630c04e90de3d9b005e7147ead75ad5.png)

In our case, we are given that $m=2,$ $n=4,$ and $m-r=1.$ 

Substituting $m=2$ into $m-r=1,$ we can find the rank of $A:$

$$
(2)-r=1\,⟹\,r=1
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) & =r=1.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given that $m=9,$ $n=4,$ and $r=2.$

$$
